entries.title: Body weight follows energy balance, but it moves slowly
entries.take: Eat above what you burn and weight rises, eat below and it falls, but the change takes months to show its full size.
entries.body: A mathematical model of adult metabolism found that body weight responds slowly to a change in intake, with a half time of about one year. It also estimated that a persistent gap of only about 30 kJ (7 kcal) a day lies behind the average weight gain seen in the US. In a ward study of 20 adults, weight change tracked energy intake closely (r = 0.8). Small daily gaps add up, and a single day rarely shows.
do: Judge a calorie target over weeks, not days.

entries.title: Calorie calculators give a starting point, not your maintenance
entries.take: Even the best resting-rate equation is within 10 percent of measured for most people, and many individuals fall outside it.
entries.body: A systematic review compared four equations for resting metabolic rate. Mifflin-St Jeor predicted within 10 percent of the measured value for more people than the others, and it still missed for a share of individuals. Total daily need is that resting figure multiplied by an activity level, and the FAO/WHO/UNU report gives about 1.40 to 2.40 as the range sustained by free-living adults. A wide range of activity levels means a wide range of totals.
do: Eat your estimate for two to three weeks while weighing yourself daily.
Adjust by 100 to 200 kcal if weight moves the wrong way.

entries.title: Most lifters do well on 1.6 to 2.2 g of protein per kg a day
entries.take: About 1.6 to 2.2 g per kg (0.7 to 1.0 g per lb) of body weight a day covers most people who lift to build muscle.
entries.body: The ISSN position stand calls 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg a day sufficient for most exercising people. A meta-analysis of 74 trials found added protein helped lean mass in adults under 65 who ate 1.6 g/kg or more. A dose-response review of 105 trials (5,402 participants) found each extra 0.1 g/kg added 0.39 kg of lean mass below 1.3 g/kg a day and 0.12 kg above it. Returns shrink as intake rises.
do: Set a daily target in grams from your body weight, then check it weekly.
Take the lower half of the range if food budget is tight.

entries.title: High protein does not harm kidney function in healthy adults
entries.take: In healthy adults without kidney disease, higher protein intakes did not reduce kidney filtration in trials.
entries.body: A meta-analysis pooled 28 trials with 1,358 participants who ate 1.5 g/kg a day or more, or at least 20 percent of energy, against lower intakes. Filtration rate was slightly higher after high-protein eating, and the change from baseline did not differ between groups. The trials were short and had some risk of selection bias. This does not cover people who already have kidney disease. They should ask their clinician.
do: If you have kidney disease or a family history, check your protein plan with a clinician first.

entries.title: Spread protein over several meals, but the split matters less than the total
entries.take: About 0.25 to 0.55 g per kg per meal is a sound target (20 to 40 g for most people), and the daily total is what matters most.
entries.body: The ISSN stand suggests 0.25 g/kg or 20 to 40 g per serving, spread across the day. A bodybuilding review pairs 1.6 to 2.2 g/kg a day with 0.40 to 0.55 g/kg per meal over 3 to 6 meals. Muscle protein synthesis levelled off at about 0.24 g/kg in younger men and 0.40 g/kg in older men. In eight adults, even meals raised 24-hour synthesis 25 percent more than a skewed pattern. A review calls the distribution evidence limited and inconsistent, and a tracer study found 100 g produced a larger, longer response than 25 g, so there is no hard cap per meal.
do: Aim for three to five protein-containing meals.
Do not worry about one bigger protein meal.

entries.title: Protein timing around training matters little next to the daily total
entries.take: Eating protein straight after training is fine, but a precise window does not change results once daily intake is met.
entries.body: A systematic review of 65 studies with 2,907 participants found protein supplementation raised lean body mass in adults and older adults, and subgroup analyses showed no benefit from any specific timing. The ISSN position says the anabolic effect of exercise lasts at least 24 hours. A protein-containing meal before or after training is a reasonable habit, and it is not urgent.
do: Eat a protein meal within a few hours either side of training.

entries.title: Plant protein builds muscle about as well, given enough total protein
entries.take: When total protein is adequate, plant and animal sources give similar muscle and strength gains over months.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 18 studies found protein source did not change absolute lean mass or strength, though animal protein favoured percent lean mass, and younger adults gained 0.41 kg more lean mass with animal protein. In a 12-week trial, 19 vegans and 19 omnivores on 1.6 g/kg gained muscle alike. A soy-versus-animal meta-analysis of nine studies agreed. Single-meal studies do show a lower response to soy and wheat, which is why total intake matters.
do: If you eat no animal foods, aim for the upper half of the protein range.
Mix soy, legumes and grains across the day.

entries.title: Carbohydrate boosts lifting only in long, high-volume sessions
entries.take: Carbohydrate intake had little effect on strength training in short fed sessions, and may help when volume is high.
entries.body: A systematic review of 49 studies found that carbohydrate intake per se is unlikely to change strength training performance in a fed state in workouts of up to 10 sets per muscle group. Acute gains showed up mostly in fasted comparisons and higher volumes. For long or very hard sessions, a sports nutrition review gives 30 to 60 g an hour during sessions of more than an hour. Physique-athlete reviews suggest at least 3 to 5 g/kg a day.
do: After protein and fat are set, fill the rest of your calories with carbohydrate you enjoy.

entries.title: Keep fat from falling too low: about 15 to 30 percent of calories
entries.take: Fat of roughly 0.5 to 1.5 g per kg, or 15 to 30 percent of energy, is a sound band, and very low fat has costs.
entries.body: Reviews for lean physique athletes suggest 15 to 30 percent of calories from fat, or 0.5 to 1.5 g/kg in the off-season, with a low end of 10 to 25 percent in contest preparation. A meta-analysis of six trials (206 men) found low-fat diets lowered total testosterone (standardised difference -0.38) against high-fat diets. This is mainly a floor for hormones and diet quality, not a target to push higher.
do: Do not cut fat below about 0.5 g per kg of body weight for long.

entries.title: Aim for 25 to 29 g of fibre a day
entries.take: In large analyses, health benefits from fibre were greatest at about 25 to 29 g a day, with more possibly better.
entries.body: A series of meta-analyses covered 185 prospective studies and 58 trials with 4,635 adults. Observational data suggested 15 to 30 percent lower all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in the highest fibre eaters against the lowest, and trials showed lower body weight, blood pressure and cholesterol with more fibre. Risk reduction was greatest at 25 to 29 g a day. Raise intake gradually and drink fluids with it.
do: Add fibre slowly over a few weeks.

entries.title: Pre-workout eating helps in long sessions, and little else about timing is critical
entries.take: Daily totals decide results, and a meal before training mostly helps if you train fasted or do high volume.
entries.body: The joint position stand of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada and the ACSM says performance and recovery improve with well-chosen type, amount and timing of food and fluids. In the carbohydrate review, the acute benefits appeared mostly in fasted comparisons and workouts above 10 sets per muscle group. Physique reviews suggest a protein dose of 0.4 to 0.5 g/kg before and after sessions as a convenient pattern.
do: Eat a normal meal one to three hours before hard sessions.

entries.title: Being under-hydrated lowers strength and muscle endurance
entries.take: Hypohydration reduced strength by about 5.5 percent and muscle endurance by about 8 percent in a meta-analysis.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 28 papers found hypohydration, meaning a body fluid deficit, cut muscle endurance by 8.3 percent, strength by 5.5 percent and anaerobic power by 5.8 percent. Dehydrating by exercise hurt more than passive methods, and trained people tended to lose less. This is about ordinary fluid habits. Deliberate dehydration to make a weight class is risky and needs an experienced coach and clinician.
do: Start sessions well hydrated and drink during long or hot ones.
Never use extreme dehydration to change weight quickly.

entries.title: Heavy drinking after hard training blunts the muscle repair signal
entries.take: A very large dose of alcohol after training cut muscle protein synthesis by 24 to 37 percent in one small study.
entries.body: Eight active men did a hard session of legs and cycling, then drank alcohol at 1.5 g/kg (about 12 standard drinks) with either protein or carbohydrate. Muscle protein synthesis was 24 percent lower with alcohol and protein, and 37 percent lower with alcohol and carbohydrate, than with protein alone. That is one small study at a heavy dose. Effects of one or two drinks were not tested.
do: Keep drinking light on the days you most want to recover.

entries.title: Alcohol adds calories that people do not offset by eating less
entries.take: Across 22 studies, people did not eat less after drinking, so total energy for the day rose.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 22 studies with 701 participants found no compensation for alcoholic energy: food intake rose by 343 kJ (about 82 kcal), and total energy intake rose by 1,072 kJ (about 256 kcal). Alcohol itself provides 7 kcal per gram on the standard Atwater scale, between carbohydrate and fat. Counting drinks in your log is the only way to see this.
do: Log drinks like food, and count mixers.

entries.title: Creatine monohydrate is the best-supported lifting supplement
entries.take: Taking 3 to 5 g of creatine monohydrate a day adds lean mass when combined with training, and it is safe for healthy people.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 35 trials with 1,192 participants found creatine added 1.10 kg of lean mass when combined with resistance training. Men gained 1.46 kg, and women a non-significant 0.29 kg, though women were fewer in the data. The ISSN position stand finds supplementation up to 30 g a day for 5 years safe in healthy people. The 3 to 5 g daily dose comes from a physique-athlete review. In 31 men, 3 g a day raised muscle creatine over 28 days by about as much as 20 g a day did in 6 days.
do: Take 3 to 5 g of creatine monohydrate every day.

entries.title: Caffeine gives a small, real boost to strength and power
entries.take: In a meta-analysis, caffeine raised maximal strength and power slightly, mostly in the upper body.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 10 studies on strength and 10 on power found caffeine improved both (standardised differences 0.20 and 0.17). The effect was significant for upper-body strength, and not for lower-body. The review also notes poor blinding and little data for women. The ISSN's 2010 stand found about 3 to 6 mg/kg effective, with no further gain at 9 mg/kg or more; a bodybuilding review lists 5 to 6 mg/kg.
do: Test your dose in training before a key session.

entries.title: Beta-alanine and citrulline help in specific cases, with modest effects
entries.take: Beta-alanine helps efforts of one to four minutes, and citrulline malate added about three reps per exercise.
entries.body: The ISSN stand says 4 to 6 g of beta-alanine daily for two to four weeks improves exercise performance, most clearly in tasks lasting 1 to 4 minutes, and tingling, the main side effect, is reduced by splitting the dose into amounts of about 1.6 g. A meta-analysis of eight studies (137 participants) found 6 to 8 g of citrulline malate taken 40 to 60 minutes before lifting added about 3 repetitions (6.4 percent). Both effects are small next to training and sleep.
do: Consider these only after protein, creatine and training are in place.

entries.title: Most supplements lack good evidence, and some carry risks
entries.take: The IOC finds only a few supplements, including caffeine and creatine, have good evidence, and the rest are unproven.
entries.body: The IOC consensus says nutrition makes a small but valuable contribution and few supplements have good evidence of benefit; some risk contamination with banned substances. BCAA pills have no human studies of oral BCAA alone on muscle synthesis. A review of 50 testosterone-booster products found no testosterone data for 61.5 percent of them, and data showing a rise for 24.8 percent.
do: Buy from brands with third-party testing if you compete in a tested sport.

entries.title: Logging food is linked to better results, and frequency matters most
entries.take: People who logged more often lost more, and a rough log kept consistently beats a perfect one kept rarely.
entries.body: A systematic review of 22 studies found a significant association between self-monitoring and weight loss, though the evidence was weak because of method limits. In a 24-week program of 142 people, those losing 5 percent or more of their weight logged in 2.4 times a day against 1.6 for the rest, and time per day fell from about 23 to 15 minutes. These are observational links, not proof logging causes the loss.
do: Log at the time you eat, and aim for most days, not perfect days.

entries.title: US labels may legally run up to 20 percent above the declared calories
entries.take: A US food is misbranded only if its calories exceed the declared value by more than 20 percent.
entries.body: Under 21 CFR 101.9(g)(5), a food is deemed misbranded if the measured calories, sugars, fat, saturated fat, trans fat, cholesterol or sodium exceed the label by more than 20 percent. Measured snack foods did better than that: in 24 products the median was 4.3 percent above the label, in the legal range. Other countries have their own tolerances, so check yours. Treat any label as an estimate.
do: Expect small errors, and weigh food rather than trust serving counts.

entries.title: Under-reporting is the norm, even among athletes and dietitians
entries.take: Self-reported intake is usually below true intake, by around a fifth in athletes and by more in some groups.
entries.body: A systematic review of 59 studies of 6,298 adults, using doubly labeled water as the reference, found most reported significant under-reporting. In athletes, intake was 19 percent too low on average. In 20 women, dietitians under-reported by 223 kcal a day and controls by 429. Ten people who said they could not lose weight on under 1,200 kcal actually under-reported by 47 percent, a small group.
do: If weight is not changing, assume your log is low before blaming metabolism.

entries.title: Tracking can feed disordered eating in people who are prone to it
entries.take: Calorie apps are linked to more eating-disorder symptoms in surveys, and many patients blame them.
entries.body: Among 105 people diagnosed with an eating disorder, about 75 percent used My Fitness Pal and 73 percent of those said it contributed to their illness. In 122 men, app users had higher eating-disorder symptoms than non-users, and 493 students showed the same link. These are cross-sectional surveys, so the app may attract people already at risk. Take the signal seriously either way.
do: Stop tracking and talk to a clinician if logging brings guilt, fear or rules you cannot break.

entries.title: Hand portions are a rougher but gentler way to estimate food
entries.take: Using your hand as a ruler reached within 25 percent of the true weight for most simple foods in one study.
entries.body: In 67 adults who estimated 42 pre-weighed foods, a finger-width method put 80 percent of geometric foods within 25 percent of true weight and 13 percent within 10 percent. Household cups and spoons managed 29 percent within 25 percent. A review of physique sport recommends flexible eating and structured monitoring to lower mental health risk. Hand portions suit people who find weighing food stressful.
do: Use palm, fist, cupped hand and thumb, and check once against a scale.

entries.title: Weighing cooked food but logging the raw entry
entries.take: Raw and cooked weights differ by the water gained or lost, so the entry must match the state you weighed.
entries.body: Rice, pasta and oats take up water when cooked and weigh more, while meat loses water and weighs less. A raw entry logged for cooked food (or the reverse) can be off by a large margin. Pick one habit: weigh raw before cooking, or choose a database entry that says cooked.
do: Weigh food in the state the database entry names.
Weigh dry foods before they cook when you can.

entries.title: Forgetting cooking oil and butter
entries.take: Fat has 9 kcal per gram, so a splash of oil in the pan can add a few hundred calories unseen.
entries.body: Fat provides 9 kcal per gram on the Atwater scale, so 10 g of oil adds about 90 kcal and a generous 25 g pour adds about 225. Oil is the classic missing entry in a log because it never sits on the plate as a measured item.
do: Measure oil with a spoon or weigh the pan before and after.
Log sauces and dressings the same way.

entries.title: Eyeballing dense foods like nut butter, cheese and cereal
entries.take: Eyeballed portions of calorie-dense foods are easy to get wrong, and small errors there cost the most calories.
entries.body: In a study of 67 adults, estimates of pre-weighed foods using cups and spoons landed within 25 percent of the true weight only 29 percent of the time. The foods that hide energy, such as nut butter or granola, have the most calories per gram, so small errors cost more. Weigh these items, and eyeball vegetables if you like.
do: Weigh the dense foods; estimate the low-calorie ones.

entries.title: Taking the first database entry without checking it
entries.take: App databases are good on average but hold wrong and duplicate entries that can swing a meal by hundreds of calories.
entries.body: A validation of MyFitnessPal in 50 participants found cleaned values matched a lab database well for energy (r=0.96), but 2.8 percent of entries had to be removed as implausible, using a 1,500 kcal per portion ceiling. A comparison of five apps found values for some nutrients, including protein and fat, lower than research software. Barcode scans are as good as the product record behind them.
do: Compare the entry to the packet label.
Prefer entries from the manufacturer, and delete odd ones.

entries.title: Not logging drinks, bites, tastes and sauces
entries.take: Small unlogged items are a large part of why logs read low.
entries.body: Under-reporting against doubly labeled water is common, but the reviews do not say which items go missing, so this is a practical reading and not a measured split. Milk in coffee, juice, snacks while cooking, and sauces add up across a week.
do: Log as you go, not at the end of the day.
Count liquid calories too.

entries.title: Logging a restaurant meal at the number on the menu
entries.take: Restaurant meals often hold more energy than stated, and the error is largest on individual items.
entries.body: Laboratory analysis of 269 foods from 42 restaurants found the average stated value was close, but 19 percent of items contained at least 100 kcal more than stated. In 29 reduced-energy restaurant foods, measured energy averaged 18 percent above stated, and free side dishes pushed it far higher. Non-chain restaurant meals averaged about 1,205 kcal. A generous estimate is safer than a hopeful one.
do: Add 10 to 20 percent for restaurant meals when your goal is losing weight.

entries.title: Tracking weekdays carefully and weekends loosely
entries.take: Weekend eating and activity can erase much of a weekday deficit.
entries.body: In 48 adults, weight rose on weekend days at baseline, and in the calorie-restriction group weight loss stopped on weekends. An analysis of 4,657 weights from 80 adults found weight higher on Sunday and Monday, decreasing through the week, which is normal and not by itself a sign of gain. People who compensated most were most likely to lose or maintain.
do: Log the weekend with the same effort, or compare weekly averages.

entries.title: Treating the tracker as exact, or quitting after one bad day
entries.take: Tracker numbers are estimates with real error, and a single high day changes little.
entries.body: Labels, databases, restaurant meals, wearables and your own memory all carry error, and wearable energy estimates vary widely with the activity. The log is useful for trends. A missed day or an over-target day matters little against weeks of data, and dropping the log altogether is the larger loss.
do: Use a weekly average and adjust slowly.
Restart the next meal, not the next Monday.

entries.title: Daily protein for lifters
entries.take: The common target for building muscle: 0.7 to 1.0 g per lb a day.

entries.title: Protein per serving
entries.take: ISSN guide: 0.25 g per kg, or 20 to 40 g, a serving. A bodybuilding review suggests 0.40 to 0.55 g per kg per meal.

entries.title: Energy per gram of food
entries.take: Protein 4, carbohydrate 4, fat 9 and alcohol 7 kcal per gram on food labels.

entries.title: Accuracy of the best equation
entries.take: Mifflin-St Jeor was within 10 percent of measured resting rate for the most people.

entries.title: Activity multiplier range
entries.take: Long-term sustainable activity levels for free-living adults, per FAO/WHO/UNU.

entries.title: US label tolerance
entries.take: A food is misbranded only above this; a typical snack runs a few percent over.

entries.title: Under-reporting in athletes
entries.take: Self-reported energy intake was this much lower than measured expenditure.

entries.title: Creatine monohydrate dose
entries.take: Daily dose from a physique-athlete review; lean-mass gain was about 1.1 kg with training.

entries.title: Caffeine dose often studied
entries.take: ISSN 2010: about 3 to 6 mg per kg works, 9 or more adds nothing; 5 mg/kg is 2.3 mg per lb. Half-life was 7.9 h on low-dose oral contraceptives, 5.4 h without.

entries.title: Fibre target
entries.take: Intake at which health benefits were greatest in pooled studies.

entries.title: Maintenance calories
entries.take: The daily energy intake at which your body weight stays steady over weeks. Also called total daily energy expenditure.

entries.title: Resting metabolic rate (RMR)
entries.take: The energy your body uses at rest to keep you alive, usually 60 to 70 percent of a day for inactive people, estimated by equations or measured.

entries.title: Thermic effect of food (TEF)
entries.take: The energy used to digest, absorb and store food, about 5 to 15 percent of daily energy expenditure on a mixed diet, and higher with protein and alcohol.

entries.title: Atwater factors
entries.take: Standard energy values per gram that food labels use: 4 kcal for protein and carbohydrate, 9 for fat, 7 for alcohol. They are averages, not measurements of your food.

entries.title: Macronutrients (macros)
entries.take: The three nutrients that provide most energy: protein, carbohydrate and fat. Alcohol is sometimes counted as a fourth source of energy.

entries.title: Leucine
entries.take: An essential amino acid that acts as a trigger for muscle protein synthesis. Animal proteins contain more than most plant proteins, per gram of protein.

entries.title: Kilojoule (kJ) and kilocalorie (kcal)
entries.take: Two units of food energy. One kcal, the calorie on most labels, equals 4.184 kJ. Many countries print kJ.

entries.title: Ergogenic aid
entries.take: Something taken to improve exercise performance or training results. Creatine and caffeine are the best-supported examples.

entries.title: Protein targets by goal and body weight
entries.take: Daily protein in g per kg and per lb, with worked examples for 70 kg (154 lb) and 90 kg (198 lb) people.
rows: Lean lifter in a calorie deficit

entries.title: Hand-portion guide
entries.take: A rough guide for estimating a serving with your own hand when you do not weigh food. Check it against a scale once.
rows: Thumb of cheese, small handful of nuts
Wide range: weigh these when you can

entries.title: Supplement evidence at a glance
entries.take: How the common supplements rate for people who lift, from strongest to weakest evidence.
rows: Adds lean mass and strength with training

entries.title: Essential, nonessential and conditionally essential nutrients
entries.take: Essential: needed and not made in enough amount, so food must supply it. Nonessential: needed, but the body builds its own. Conditionally essential: supply falls short only in some states; McDonald puts carbohydrate there for hard training.

entries.title: Essential fatty acids (EFAs)
entries.take: Fats the body needs but cannot build: by the textbook, linoleic acid (LA, omega-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (ALA, omega-3). McDonald's view is that almost any diet with fat covers the minimum, not the optimum. See the diet planner.

entries.title: Plant omega-3 (ALA) converted poorly to DHA in tracer studies, least in men
entries.take: In tracer studies, young men made some EPA from ALA but no measurable DHA, while young women converted about 21 percent to EPA and 9 percent to DHA.
entries.body: Six young men on their usual diet swallowed labelled ALA with a meal. EPA and DPA appeared in the blood, but no labelled DHA showed up over 21 days, and the authors judged that men may depend on DHA eaten ready-made. A matching study in young women estimated net conversion of 21 percent to EPA, 6 percent to DPA and 9 percent to DHA, which the authors linked to the needs of pregnancy. The men's study had only six people. McDonald's view is that flax and other ALA oils are a poor stand-in for fish. For omega-3 and the heart, see the omega-3 entry in the health section.
do: McDonald's practice: do not count flax or other ALA oils as your EPA and DHA.
If you want EPA and DHA, eat fatty fish or another ready-made source.

entries.title: McDonald argues arachidonic acid and DHA may be the real essential fats
entries.take: LA and ALA are the textbook essential fats, but much of what they do runs through their products. McDonald's reading is that arachidonic acid (AA) and DHA are the ones the body truly needs.
entries.body: A 1999 review held that the need for AA is the main reason omega-6 fats are essential, and that DHA, needed for vision and nerve development, is the more likely essential omega-3, though the need may be for 22-carbon omega-3 fats in general. A hospital team saw no fatty acid deficiency in patients fed by drip on a fish-oil emulsion with AA and DHA but almost no LA or ALA, and in mice AA and DHA alone prevented it. In a tracer study of nine adults, 0.3 to 0.6 percent of LA became AA. The evidence is thin and mostly not from healthy adults.

entries.title: Cutting vegetable oils for fear that omega-6 fat inflames the body
entries.take: In 15 randomised trials of healthy people, adding linoleic acid, the main omega-6 fat, did not raise blood markers of inflammation.
entries.body: The worry is that linoleic acid becomes arachidonic acid, a raw material for signals that drive inflammation. A systematic review of 15 trials (8 parallel, 7 crossover) in healthy, non-infant groups found no significant change in C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, cytokines, TNF-alpha or adhesion molecules with more linoleic acid. Two trials did see shifts in urinary eicosanoid products, which their authors did not read as more inflammation. The review covered markers, not disease. McDonald's view is that the larger gap in most modern diets is too little omega-3 rather than too much omega-6.
do: McDonald's practice: put effort into omega-3 sources; he leaves open whether omega-6 needs cutting.

entries.title: Keep industrial trans fat as close to zero as you can
entries.take: Trans fat from partially hydrogenated oils harms blood lipids, and intakes of about 2 percent of energy went with a markedly higher rate of heart disease.
entries.body: A 2009 review names partially hydrogenated vegetable oils as the main source in most countries. Trans fat worsened blood lipids and raised markers of inflammation and poor blood vessel function, and some studies linked it to visceral fat and insulin resistance. In observational data, even about 2 percent of energy from trans fat went with markedly more coronary heart disease. Links with diabetes were less consistent. McDonald treats this as the rare fat question with no real debate.
do: Check ingredient lists for partially hydrogenated oil and choose another product.

entries.title: Most adults with lactose intolerance tolerated about a cup of milk's lactose
entries.take: In a systematic review, 12 to 15 g of lactose, roughly one cup of milk, was well tolerated by most adults with lactose intolerance or malabsorption.
entries.body: Lactose, the sugar in milk, is split by the enzyme lactase. Without enough lactase it reaches the colon and ferments, causing gas and loose stools. The review of 36 trials rated the cup-of-milk finding moderate quality, but most trials enrolled people with malabsorption rather than diagnosed intolerance, and evidence for lactose-reduced milk, probiotics or gradual adaptation was too thin to judge. Milk allergy is a different, immune reaction to milk protein, and this figure does not apply to it. See also the dairy entry in the diet section.
do: If dairy upsets your stomach, have it assessed by a clinician before cutting it out.
With a milk allergy, follow your allergist's advice, not the tolerance figure.

entries.title: Energy from dietary fibre
entries.take: FAO factor for fibre in ordinary foods, from gut bacteria fermenting part of it. Fibre they cannot ferment gives none.

entries.title: On a proposed net energy scale, protein counts for less than its label value
entries.take: Labels count protein at 4 kcal (17 kJ) per gram. On a net energy scale the FAO describes but has not adopted, it is worth 3.2 kcal (13 kJ).
entries.body: Label factors (see the Atwater entry) count energy the body absorbs and does not lose in urine. The FAO also describes a net scale that subtracts heat lost in handling each nutrient, from the thermic effect (see the TEF entry) and gut fermentation. On it, protein drops from 17 to 13 kJ a gram, a 24 percent cut, fibre from 2.0 to 1.4 kcal, and fat stays at 9. For most mixed diets the total falls only 4 to 6 percent, and the FAO workshop kept the older factors. McDonald mentions the lower protein value as an open debate.
do: Keep logging with label values, since targets and databases are built on them.

entries.title: McDonald argues per-meal protein caps ignore breakdown and non-muscle tissue
entries.take: In young adults, a meal with about 70 g of protein gave better whole-body protein balance than one with 40 g, mostly by cutting protein breakdown.
entries.body: McDonald argues that per-meal caps rest on studies measuring muscle protein synthesis after one dose of protein, often whey taken alone, and that they ignore breakdown and the large share of lean mass that is not muscle. In 23 healthy young adults, net whole-body protein balance was greater after about 70 g than after 40 g, mainly through less breakdown, with or without prior lifting. That is whole-body data, not muscle. For later tracer work with larger doses, see the per-meal entry.

entries.title: In six knee-surgery patients, tendon and cartilage made protein at rates near muscle's
entries.take: In six patients having knee replacement, basal protein synthesis in tendon, ligament, cartilage and menisci did not differ significantly from muscle.
entries.body: During surgery, a labelled amino acid was infused and tissue samples taken. Rates ran from 0.02 to 0.13 percent an hour across tissues: tendon about 0.06, cruciate ligaments 0.04 to 0.07, cartilage and menisci 0.04, against 0.04 for muscle. Only synovium ran higher, and bone from the knee notch lower. The six were in their sixties and measured at rest during surgery, so this says nothing yet about training. McDonald reads it as support for his view that protein needs are not set by muscle alone.

entries.title: McDonald sets lifters at 2.2 g per kg of protein, and high-level athletes higher
entries.take: McDonald's practice: about 2.2 g per kg (1 g per lb) for recreational lifters outside a diet, and 2.5 to 3.0 g per kg (1.1 to 1.4 g per lb) for high-level strength athletes.
entries.body: His reasons are practical. People who aim at 1 g per lb tend to land below it, and he sees no harm in high intakes as long as carbohydrate and fat still fit. The evidence is less firm than the target. He draws the higher range from a 2004 review, though that review found few outcome data showing 2 to 3 g per kg is needed, and pooled trials show returns shrinking as intake rises (see the protein range entry). With kidney disease, set protein with a clinician (see the kidney entry).
do: McDonald's practice: aim at 1 g per lb, since most people land below their target.

entries.title: Higher protein did not harm bone, and may help the spine slightly
entries.take: A meta-analysis of 16 trials and 20 cohort studies found no harm to bone from higher protein, and a possible small gain in lumbar spine density.
entries.body: In McDonald's account, the worry began with early studies feeding purified protein, which saw calcium lost from the body. The pooled analysis found lumbar spine density may be 0.52 percent higher with more protein, from five trials, and no effect at the hip, femoral neck or whole body. Limited evidence did not support an extra benefit from protein combined with calcium and vitamin D, the pairing his 2007 article leans on; the analysis came later. Studies varied, and confounding could not be ruled out.

entries.title: Essential amino acids and leucine in common protein powders
entries.take: Share of the protein in each isolate, measured in one lab. A dash means the figure was not in the summary. Plant isolates vary widely, and blends of them can come close to animal profiles.

entries.title: PDCAAS (protein digestibility-corrected amino acid score)
entries.take: A protein quality score adopted by FAO/WHO in 1991. It compares a protein's essential amino acids with a reference pattern for young children, corrects for digestibility over the whole gut, and is capped at 1.0, so top proteins tie.

entries.title: DIAAS (digestible indispensable amino acid score)
entries.take: The score FAO has recommended in place of PDCAAS. It uses the digestibility of each essential amino acid at the end of the small intestine and is not capped. In rats it ran from 0.01 for a corn cereal to 1.18 for milk protein concentrate.

entries.title: Ranking protein sources by quality score when you already eat plenty
entries.take: McDonald's view is that quality scores matter most for diets short of protein, and that at a lifter's intake from mixed sources, gaps between good proteins matter little.
entries.body: The authors of one scoring study say the gap between methods matters most where protein intake is marginal. In pigs, the older method rated skimmed milk powder, soy, pea and wheat higher than the newer one, and in rats it ran higher mainly for poorer proteins, so plant scores need care when one plant source carries a low intake. Plant isolates also differ widely in amino acids (see the amino acid table). For plant and animal protein over months, see the plant protein entry.
do: McDonald's practice: hit your daily protein total first, then think about the source.

entries.title: Fast and slow proteins
entries.take: Proteins whose amino acids reach the blood at different speeds. Whey gives a sharp, short rise in blood amino acids; casein gives a lower rise that lasts for hours, probably because it leaves the stomach slowly.

entries.title: Whey and casein differ most when eaten alone, less in a mixed meal
entries.take: In a single-protein meal, casein left more protein in the body over 7 hours than whey did. Early results suggest added carbohydrate and fat narrow the gap.
entries.body: In the first study, whey raised whole-body protein synthesis by 68 percent and burned more amino acids, while casein cut protein breakdown by 34 percent; net leucine balance over 7 hours favoured casein. That was whole-body data in rested adults, not muscle after training, and McDonald's article adds that the protein was taken alone after an overnight fast. The same group's preliminary results found added fat and carbohydrate blunted the differences, and they suggest a fast protein may suit older people better.
do: McDonald's practice: before or during training, take quick-digesting whey, since slow protein sits in the gut.

entries.title: After whole-body training, 40 g of whey beat 20 g for muscle protein synthesis
entries.take: In 30 resistance-trained young men, 40 g of whey after a whole-body session raised muscle protein synthesis about 20 percent more than 20 g, whatever their lean mass.
entries.body: The accepted ceiling was 20 to 25 g, and McDonald's article says that figure came from leg-only training. Here men with lean mass of 65 kg (143 lb) or less and 70 kg (154 lb) or more did a whole-body session, then took 20 or 40 g of whey. Synthesis rose from 0.049 to 0.059 percent an hour with the larger dose, and lean mass made no difference. McDonald's view is that doubling the dose bought a modest gain, but his article notes only the thigh was sampled, so the other trained muscles may have gained too. See the per-meal entry.
do: After a full-body session, consider nearer 40 g than 20 g; the evidence is one short study.

entries.title: Eating eggs raw for their protein
entries.take: In five people with an ileostomy, about 51 percent of raw egg protein was absorbed by the end of the small intestine, against 91 percent when cooked.
entries.body: Digestibility is the share of eaten protein the gut takes in. Each person ate 25 g of labelled egg protein once cooked and once raw, and heating raised digestibility sharply. The study was tiny and used a measurement taken at the end of the small intestine, but the gap was large. McDonald also warns that raw eggs carry a risk of salmonella food poisoning.
do: Cook eggs before you eat them.

entries.title: Without animal foods, plan for vitamin B12, and expect less iron to be absorbed
entries.take: B12 depletion was common among vegetarians, more so vegans. In people with no iron stores, about 5 to 12 percent of iron is absorbed from vegetarian diets, 14 to 18 from mixed.
entries.body: A review of 18 studies of vegetarians found B12 deficiency in 62 percent of pregnant women, 25 to 86 percent of children, 21 to 41 of adolescents and 11 to 90 of older people, and its authors advise regular B12 supplements. The iron figures are estimates. Phytate, polyphenols, calcium, vitamin C and meat changed iron absorption in single-meal studies, less so across varied diets, and iron status matters more than diet. McDonald's view is that lean red meat is a strong source of iron and zinc, and that athletes who drop it, women especially, risk running short.
do: If you eat no animal foods, ask a clinician or dietitian about a B12 source and testing.
Take iron only after a blood test and a clinician's advice (see the women's iron entry); McDonald warns excess harms men.

entries.title: Soluble, insoluble and fermentable fibre
entries.take: Soluble (viscous) fibre forms a gel in water and slows stomach emptying. Insoluble fibre does not dissolve and adds bulk. Fermentable fibre is broken down by gut bacteria into gases and short-chain fatty acids, which supply some energy.

entries.title: McDonald warns that high fibre can work against big eaters
entries.take: More fibre lowered how much fat and protein the gut absorbed in a feeding study. McDonald's view is that this and the fullness help dieters and hinder big eaters.
entries.body: In 17 people on controlled diets, each eaten for two weeks, raising fibre lowered fat and protein digestibility and the usable energy of the diet. McDonald's estimate is that going from about 18 to 36 g of fibre a day costs around 100 kcal absorbed, an effect he says is not large. His general starting point is 5 to 10 g of fibre a meal. For lifters trying to gain or athletes who burn a great deal, his concern is that bulk and lost absorption make eating enough harder.
do: McDonald's practice: if you struggle to eat enough, eat the salad or vegetables last.

entries.title: Glycaemic load (GL)
entries.take: A food's glycaemic index multiplied by the grams of carbohydrate in the portion eaten, divided by 100. It accounts for both the kind and the amount of carbohydrate (see the glycaemic index entry in the diet guide).

entries.title: Ruling out a food for its glycaemic index without looking at the portion
entries.take: GI is measured on a serving that holds 50 g of available carbohydrate, so a high value says little about a vegetable eaten in small amounts.
entries.body: In a GI test, fasted volunteers eat enough of a food to provide 50 g of available carbohydrate. For foods low in carbohydrate that can mean an unrealistic plate: McDonald's estimate for carrots is about a dozen medium ones. Glycaemic load scales GI by the carbohydrate actually eaten, and the international tables list it for stated serving sizes. McDonald's view is that banning carrots or similar foods over their GI makes no sense.
do: McDonald's practice: judge a vegetable by the portion you eat, not by its GI alone.

entries.title: A lower glycaemic index does not always mean less insulin
entries.take: In six healthy men, a low-GI bran cereal raised insulin sooner than high-GI corn flakes. Its lower GI came from faster glucose removal, not slower entry.
entries.body: Both cereals supplied 50 g of available carbohydrate, and glucose entered the blood at a similar rate. With the bran cereal, insulin was 76 percent higher at 20 minutes and glucose left the blood faster, which flattened the curve. In 30 people with type 2 diabetes, adding about 21 g of protein to 50 g of a slowly digested sugar raised insulin by roughly 190 to 270 percent, but insulin action fell and the glucose response did not change. McDonald's view is that choosing foods by GI to keep insulin down rests on a false assumption.

entries.title: The same cereal scored a different glycaemic index in trained and sedentary men
entries.take: One breakfast cereal's GI differed by about 23 units between endurance-trained and sedentary young men, so a published value may not fit everyone.
entries.body: In 34 young men with normal glucose tolerance, moderately trained men fell between the two groups, and the insulin index did not differ. An earlier study by the same team found the gap for one of three cereals, with a second close to significance. McDonald's reading is that GI runs lower in trained people, and he puts this down to their better insulin sensitivity.

entries.title: Lowering glycaemic index or load added nothing to a calorie deficit in a feeding trial
entries.take: In 29 adults with obesity on provided food for 12 weeks, high-GI, low-GI and high-fat diets with the same deficit lost similar weight.
entries.body: Each diet sat about 3,138 kJ (750 kcal) a day below estimated needs. Losses were 9.3, 9.9 and 8.4 kg, with no difference, and insulin sensitivity improved on all three; 22 people kept their losses over 24 weeks of free living. A report from the CALERIE trial in overweight adults found a low-GL diet helped only those with high insulin secretion. McDonald reads the low-GL weight-loss research as mixed, and argues that such diets also change fibre and protein.
do: Set the calorie deficit first and treat GI as a minor detail.

entries.title: Carbohydrate eaten straight after hard exercise refills glycogen fastest
entries.take: After depleting exercise, glycogen refilled fastest with carbohydrate taken at once, and a delay of hours could halve the rate. McDonald thinks this matters mainly for same-day sessions.
entries.body: A review of short-term recovery found the highest muscle glycogen synthesis with about 1.0 to 1.85 g/kg of carbohydrate an hour, started straight after exercise and repeated every 15 to 60 minutes for up to 5 hours. A delay of several hours may cut the rate by about half. Added protein raised synthesis only when carbohydrate was under about 1.2 g/kg an hour. McDonald's view is that with a day between hard sessions for the same muscles, timing and GI make no real difference, and he keeps fast, high-GI refuelling for sessions six to eight hours apart.
do: With two hard sessions in one day, eat carbohydrate soon after the first.

entries.title: Carbohydrate loading helps in endurance events of more than about 90 minutes
entries.take: Raising muscle glycogen above normal delayed fatigue by about 20 percent in events over 90 minutes, and did not help efforts under 5 minutes or runs and rides of 60 to 90.
entries.body: A 1997 review found that after 60 to 90 minutes of moderate running or cycling, plenty of glycogen is still left in the working muscles, so extra stores add nothing. Beyond 90 minutes, exhaustion tended to coincide with very low muscle glycogen. In races over a set distance, high-carbohydrate diets improved performance by 2 to 3 percent. McDonald's view is that a recreational 5 km runner gains nothing from loading and may only carry extra water, and that slower marathoners, out on the course longest, are the ones at risk of running low.
do: For events under an hour, eat your normal diet beforehand instead of loading.

entries.title: A short all-out effort and one day of high carbohydrate loaded glycogen in a small study
entries.take: In seven endurance-trained athletes, 3 minutes of very hard cycling then 24 hours at about 10 g/kg of high-GI carbohydrate nearly doubled muscle glycogen.
entries.body: Published loading plans took two to six days; McDonald's article recounts that the first versions began with several days of low carbohydrate and hard training. Here athletes rode 150 seconds at 130 percent of peak aerobic capacity, then 30 seconds all out, and ate 10.3 g of carbohydrate per kg of body weight over the next day. Glycogen rose from about 109 to 198 mmol/kg wet weight, similar to or above longer plans. It was seven people with no comparison group. McDonald's view is that the total carbohydrate eaten matters more than which plan delivers it.
do: McDonald's practice: test any pre-race meal in training, never for the first time on race day.

entries.title: Bodybuilders who carb-loaded before a show measured bigger, and many had diarrhoea
entries.take: After three low-carbohydrate days, 15 male bodybuilders who loaded for 24 hours gained muscle thickness and photo scores; 9 who did not load had no change in thickness or girths.
entries.body: The study compared men who did and did not load, with no random allocation reported. Ultrasound thickness of the elbow flexors and triceps rose with loading, as did body mass and several girths. Diarrhoea hit 7 of the 15 loaders, 4 of them severely, and constipation was common in both groups during depletion. McDonald calls the effect of loading debatable and recalls a study finding no change in muscle size; this 2019 study, which his article links, found a short-term rise. Big peak-week swings in food and fluid can bring gut upset like this, and cutting fluid risks dehydration.
do: Plan any peak-week carbohydrate load with a sports dietitian or an experienced coach.

entries.title: Drinking more than you sweat out during a long race
entries.take: In the 2002 Boston Marathon, 13 percent of 488 sampled runners finished with low blood sodium; weight gain during the race and finishing after 4 hours went with it.
entries.body: Hyponatraemia means too little sodium in the blood, and severe cases can kill. In this group, 0.6 percent had critical levels. Gaining weight while running, a sign of drinking more than was lost, went with about four times the odds, and a time over 4 hours with about seven times the odds of a time under 3:30. Sex, type of drink and anti-inflammatory painkillers were not linked. McDonald's view is that slower marathoners are the ones prone to overdrinking, since fast runners need less and have less chance to drink.
do: Weigh yourself before and after long training runs; finishing heavier means you drank too much.
Plan race drinking with a sports dietitian or clinician if you will be out over 4 hours.

entries.title: Calories from sugary drinks were not offset by eating less
entries.take: In a crossover trial, 450 kcal a day of jelly beans was matched by eating less, while the same calories as soda were simply added on and weight rose.
entries.body: Fifteen adults took 1,880 kJ (about 450 kcal) of carbohydrate a day for four weeks as soda and four weeks as jelly beans. With the solid load they ate less of everything else, a compensation of 118 percent. With soda they ate no less, and body weight and BMI rose only in that period. A review of beverages describes the same weak compensation for drinks sweetened with sugar or high-fructose corn syrup, and for alcohol (see the alcohol energy entry). McDonald's view is that the liquid form is the problem whatever the sugar, and that milk, with its protein and fat, behaves more like food.
do: McDonald's practice: swap sugary drinks for water or diet drinks (see the diet drinks claim).

entries.title: Milk did well as a drink after sweaty endurance sessions in small trials
entries.take: Low-fat milk was retained better than water or a sports drink after sweating, and chocolate milk beat a matched carbohydrate drink between two cycling bouts.
entries.body: Eleven people sweated off 1.8 percent of body mass in warm-room exercise, then drank 150 percent of the loss. Five-hour urine was about 550 to 610 ml after milk against about 1,180 to 1,210 ml after water or a sports drink, and only milk kept them in fluid balance (see the plain water claim). In nine trained male cyclists, chocolate milk and a fluid-replacement drink both gave longer time to exhaustion than a carbohydrate drink matched to the milk for carbohydrate. McDonald's view is that milk suits recovery but not drinking during exercise, and that big athletes may need extra carbohydrate and protein added.
do: After long, sweaty sessions, milk is a sound recovery drink if you tolerate lactose (see the lactose entry).

entries.title: Energy density
entries.take: Calories per gram of food. Water, fibre and air lower it; fat raises it, and so does removing water. Refined low-fat foods can still be energy dense. Low values help dieters feel full, and high values help people who must eat a lot.

entries.title: Soy did not upset thyroid hormones in healthy adults with enough iodine
entries.take: Across 18 randomised trials, soy did not change thyroid hormones and nudged TSH up very slightly. People treated for an underactive thyroid are a separate case.
entries.body: A 2019 meta-analysis found no change in free T3 or free T4 and a TSH rise of about 0.25 mIU/L, of unclear clinical meaning. An earlier review of 14 trials in healthy adults found no or only very modest effects in all but one. That review notes that soy may cut absorption of thyroid hormone medicine and raise the dose some patients need, though they need not avoid soy. Animal and lab work suggests low iodine makes soy's effect on the thyroid worse. McDonald's view is that trouble comes from very high soy intakes paired with low iodine.
do: If you take thyroid medicine and eat soy often, tell your clinician, as your dose may need checking.
If you eat a lot of soy, make sure your iodine intake is adequate.

entries.title: Soy protein and isoflavones did not change men's testosterone
entries.take: A meta-analysis of 41 studies found no effect of soy foods, soy protein or isoflavone extracts on testosterone or oestrogen in men, at any dose or duration tested.
entries.body: Total testosterone was measured in 1,753 men and oestradiol in 1,000. Total and free testosterone, oestradiol, oestrone and SHBG did not change, and splitting the studies by isoflavone dose and length found no effect either. McDonald's 2009 article agrees that moderate intakes left testosterone alone, but argues that large daily intakes can cause problems and suggests a cap of about 20 to 25 g of soy protein a day. This later analysis found no dose effect on these hormones, though it did not look at other outcomes.
do: Men can use soy as a protein source without worrying about testosterone.

entries.title: Isoflavones (soy phytoestrogens)
entries.take: Plant compounds in soy, chiefly genistein and daidzein, that bind oestrogen receptors and can act like oestrogen. Phytoestrogen is the wider term for such plant compounds. They drive most worries about soy and hormones.

entries.title: High-fructose corn syrup behaves much like table sugar
entries.take: HFCS and sucrose are both mixes of fructose and glucose, and in 34 adults they gave similar 24-hour glucose, insulin, leptin and blood fat profiles.
entries.body: McDonald's article lists the common forms, HFCS-42 and HFCS-55, named for their fructose percentage; sucrose is half fructose. A review found HFCS no different in any meaningful way from sucrose, honey or juice concentrates, and judged the idea that it uniquely drives obesity unsupported. In eight of the men, though, blood fats after HFCS or sucrose drinks rose about as high as after pure fructose. McDonald's view is that the problem is the calories and the soft drinks that carry HFCS, not the syrup itself (see the liquid calories entry).
do: Count HFCS as added sugar, the same as sucrose or honey.

entries.title: Fructose intake below which blood fats did not rise after meals
entries.take: In pooled trials of pure fructose, under 50 g a day had no clear effect on blood fats after meals, and fasting levels and body weight held up to 100 g.

entries.title: Choose lower-mercury fish, above all in pregnancy and for children
entries.take: US FDA and EPA advice lists seven fish to avoid for their mercury, such as swordfish, shark and orange roughy, and many low-mercury picks such as salmon and sardines.
entries.body: The advice is written for people who are or may become pregnant or breastfeeding, and for children. In pregnancy and breastfeeding it suggests 2 to 3 servings of 4 oz (113 g) a week from its best-choices list, or 1 from its good-choices list; children get 2 smaller best-choice servings. Canned light tuna is a best choice and albacore a good choice; bigeye tuna, king mackerel, marlin and Gulf of Mexico tilefish are on the avoid list. McDonald's view is that lifters who eat large daily amounts of tuna or other high-mercury fish can go past the safety limits.
do: If you are pregnant or planning to be, plan your fish intake with your clinician or midwife.
McDonald's practice: if you eat fish most days, favour low-mercury kinds over large daily amounts of tuna.

entries.title: High-dose vitamins C and E blunted some training adaptations in trials
entries.take: In two randomised trials, daily vitamin C and E dulled muscle markers of adaptation, though fitness and muscle growth mostly kept pace with placebo.
entries.body: In 54 young adults doing 11 weeks of mostly running, 1,000 mg of vitamin C and 235 mg of vitamin E a day stopped the rise in markers of new mitochondria, while VO2max rose 8 percent in both groups. In 32 recreationally trained adults lifting for 10 weeks, the same doses did not change muscle growth but blunted signalling after a session and held back biceps curl strength. The authors urge caution. McDonald's view is to avoid high-dose antioxidants in main training blocks, with a possible place in a crowded competition season.
do: McDonald's practice: get antioxidants from fruit and vegetables, not high-dose pills, while training to improve.

entries.title: Taking antioxidant pills as health insurance
entries.take: In 78 randomised trials with 296,707 people, antioxidant pills did not lower deaths, and beta-carotene and vitamin E slightly raised them in the better trials.
entries.body: The Cochrane review covered beta-carotene, vitamins A, C and E, and selenium, taken for 28 days to 12 years by healthy people and patients with various diseases, mean age 63. Overall there was no clear effect on deaths. In the 56 trials at low risk of bias, deaths rose by 4 percent, beta-carotene and vitamin E raised mortality, and higher vitamin A doses went with more deaths; vitamin C and selenium showed no effect. McDonald's view is that pills cannot replace the fruit and vegetables that supply these nutrients.
do: Check any high-dose vitamin plan with a clinician or dietitian before you start.

entries.title: Many athletes test low in vitamin D, but the count depends on the cut-off
entries.take: At a cut-off of 32 ng/mL, 56 percent of 2,313 athletes were low, more in winter and in indoor sports. The IOM counts 20 ng/mL as enough for nearly everyone.
entries.body: The meta-analysis pooled 23 studies; risk above 40 degrees north rose only once Middle East studies were excluded, and any link to injury was unclear. The Institute of Medicine's 2011 report set an adult RDA of 600 IU a day (800 IU over 70), tied to a blood level of at least 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L). It found higher levels gave no consistent extra benefit, saw some risk at both extremes, and judged deficiency overestimated. McDonald's articles aim for higher levels and treat supplements as close to essential for indoor athletes. For trial results on vitamin D pills, see the vitamin D entry in the health guide.
do: If you train indoors or through dark winters, ask a clinician whether a vitamin D test is worth doing.
Do not take high-dose vitamin D without a clinician's advice.

entries.title: Glutamine added no strength or lean mass in a training trial
entries.take: In 31 young adults lifting for six weeks, a large daily glutamine dose did no better than placebo for strength, lean mass or muscle breakdown.
entries.body: The glutamine group took 0.9 g per kg of lean mass a day against the same amount of maltodextrin. Both groups raised their squat by about 30 percent and bench press by about 14 percent, and lean mass rose about 2 percent in each. Urinary 3-methylhistidine, a marker of muscle protein breakdown, did not differ. McDonald agrees that glutamine does not build muscle, and he rates its evidence for immune support as mixed.

entries.title: Muscle protein synthesis rose and fell back within hours of a protein dose
entries.take: After 48 g of whey, synthesis in eight young men peaked at 45 to 90 minutes and returned to baseline while blood amino acids were still high.
entries.body: The authors call this the muscle-full effect. In 24 trained men given 80 g of whey over 12 hours after lifting, 20 g every 3 hours raised synthesis 31 to 48 percent more than 10 g every 90 minutes or 40 g every 6 hours. McDonald's view is that protein meals 3 to 5 hours apart suit muscle gain and that eating more often adds nothing. A later tracer study found a much larger dose gave a longer response, so timing depends on dose (see the protein per meal entry).
do: Space protein meals a few hours apart rather than grazing every hour.

entries.title: Protein before bed improved overnight protein balance after evening training
entries.take: In 16 young men who lifted in the evening, 40 g of casein 30 minutes before sleep was digested overnight and improved whole-body protein balance.
entries.body: All of them had 20 g of protein and 60 g of carbohydrate straight after the session. With the bedtime casein, whole-body protein synthesis rose and net balance turned positive, and muscle protein synthesis ran about 22 percent higher, a result at the edge of significance. It covered one night, so it says nothing direct about long-term growth. McDonald is unsure it matters, since a large evening meal already supplies the night, and he would not cut sleep short to eat.
do: If you train late, a protein-rich snack before bed is a reasonable option.

entries.title: A planned surplus added fat but no extra lean mass in young elite athletes
entries.take: Over 8 to 12 weeks of added strength work, elite athletes given a surplus meal plan gained more weight and fat than those eating freely, and similar lean mass.
entries.body: Thirty-nine elite athletes, about 19 years old, were randomised. The meal-plan group ate about 3,585 kcal a day against 2,964 kcal. Body weight rose 3.9 percent against 1.5 percent and fat mass 15 percent against 3 percent, while lean mass gain did not differ and one-rep maxes rose 6 to 12 percent in both. McDonald's view is that the surplus muscle gain needs is small and shrinks with training age, so extra food mostly adds fat (see the surplus entries in the diet guide).
do: McDonald's practice: check skinfolds and gym strength every two weeks and adjust intake to the results.

entries.title: Ketosis and ketone bodies
entries.take: Ketone bodies are fuels the liver makes from fat when carbohydrate is scarce; ketosis means raised blood ketones and follows fat breakdown. Diabetic ketoacidosis is a separate danger: with diabetes, see a clinician before going low-carb.

entries.title: Judging a low-carbohydrate diet by urine ketone strips
entries.take: Strips detect ketones spilling into urine, not blood levels or fat loss. McDonald's view is that they can read negative during ketosis and that fat lost is what counts.
entries.body: McDonald's view is that ketosis is defined by blood ketones, that urine readings also shift with how much you drink, and that lean, active people may make too few ketones to show. In his view ketones rise because fat is being broken down, so a darker strip does not mean faster fat loss (see the ketosis term and the ketogenic diet entries in the diet guide). People with diabetes who test ketones for medical reasons should follow their clinician, not this entry.
do: McDonald's practice: judge the diet by fat lost and muscle kept, not by strip colour.

jager-2017.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise
jager-2017.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
jager-2017.support: General recommendations are 0.25 g of a high-quality protein per kg of body weight, or an absolute dose of 20-40 g. An overall daily protein intake in the range of 1.4-2.0 g protein/kg body weight/day is sufficient for most exercising individuals.

nunes-2022.title: Systematic review and meta‐analysis of protein intake to support muscle mass and function in healthy adults
nunes-2022.journal: Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle
nunes-2022.support: Increasing daily protein ingestion may enhance gains in LBM in studies enrolling subjects in RE; significant for younger subjects (<65 years old) ingesting >=1.6 g of protein/kg/day.

tagawa-2021.title: Dose–response relationship between protein intake and muscle mass increase: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
tagawa-2021.support: A total of 5402 study participants from 105 articles. Lean body mass rose 0.39 kg per 0.1 g/kg/d below 1.3 g/kg/d and 0.12 kg above it.

iraki-2019.title: Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review
iraki-2019.support: Sufficient protein (1.6-2.2 g/kg/day) with 0.40-0.55 g/kg per meal; fat 0.5-1.5 g/kg/day; carbohydrate at least 3-5 g/kg/day; creatine monohydrate (3-5 g/day), caffeine (5-6 mg/kg), beta-alanine (3-5 g/day) and citrulline malate (8 g/day) might yield ergogenic effects.

devries-2018.title: 'Changes in Kidney Function Do Not Differ between Healthy Adults Consuming Higher- Compared with Lower- or Normal-Protein Diets: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
devries-2018.support: 28 trials with 1358 participants; HP intakes do not adversely influence kidney function on GFR in healthy adults.

moore-2014.title: Protein Ingestion to Stimulate Myofibrillar Protein Synthesis Requires Greater Relative Protein Intakes in Healthy Older Versus Younger Men
moore-2014.journal: The Journals of Gerontology: Series A
moore-2014.support: MPS reached a plateau after ingestion of 0.40 and 0.24 g/kg body mass in older and younger men.

mamerow-2014.title: Dietary Protein Distribution Positively Influences 24-h Muscle Protein Synthesis in Healthy Adults
mamerow-2014.support: 24-h mixed muscle protein fractional synthesis rate was 25% higher in the EVEN vs the SKEW protein distribution (n = 8).

hudson-2020.title: Protein Distribution and Muscle-Related Outcomes: Does the Evidence Support the Concept?
hudson-2020.support: The current evidence on the efficacy of consuming an optimal protein distribution is limited and inconsistent.

trommelen-2023.title: The anabolic response to protein ingestion during recovery from exercise has no upper limit in magnitude and duration in vivo in humans
trommelen-2023.support: Ingestion of 100 g protein results in a greater and more prolonged (>12 h) anabolic response when compared to 25 g protein.

wirth-2020.title: The Role of Protein Intake and its Timing on Body Composition and Muscle Function in Healthy Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
wirth-2020.support: Data from 65 studies with 2907 participants; no beneficial effect of a specific timing of protein intake on LBM, handgrip strength, and leg press strength.

lim-2021.title: Animal Protein versus Plant Protein in Supporting Lean Mass and Muscle Strength: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
lim-2021.support: Protein source did not affect changes in absolute lean mass or muscle strength; animal protein favoured percent lean mass, and younger adults gained more with animal protein.

hevia-2021.title: High-Protein Plant-Based Diet Versus a Protein-Matched Omnivorous Diet to Support Resistance Training Adaptations: A Comparison Between Habitual Vegans and Omnivores
hevia-2021.support: A high-protein (~1.6 g/kg/day) exclusively plant-based diet is not different from a protein-matched mixed diet in supporting muscle strength and mass accrual (19 vegans, 19 omnivores, 12 weeks).

messina-2018.title: No Difference Between the Effects of Supplementing With Soy Protein Versus Animal Protein on Gains in Muscle Mass and Strength in Response to Resistance Exercise
messina-2018.journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
messina-2018.support: Nine studies involving 266 participants; soy protein supplementation produces similar gains in strength and LBM in response to RET as whey protein.

vanvliet-2015.title: The Skeletal Muscle Anabolic Response to Plant- versus Animal-Based Protein Consumption
vanvliet-2015.support: Ingestion of plant-based proteins in soy and wheat results in a lower muscle protein synthetic response than several animal-based proteins; most plant proteins have a relatively low leucine content.

henselmans-2022.title: The Effect of Carbohydrate Intake on Strength and Resistance Training Performance: A Systematic Review
henselmans-2022.support: 49 studies; carbohydrate intake per se is unlikely to affect strength training performance in a fed state in workouts of up to 10 sets per muscle group; higher volumes may benefit.

burke-2011.title: Carbohydrates for training and competition
burke-2011.support: 30-60 g/h is an appropriate target for sports of longer duration; events >2.5 h may benefit from up to 90 g/h.

roberts-2020.title: Nutritional Recommendations for Physique Athletes
roberts-2020.support: Low-end fat intake during contest preparation of 10-25% of calories; protein 1.8-2.7 g/kg; four or five protein boluses a day.

helms-2014-prep.title: Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation
helms-2014-prep.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
helms-2014-prep.support: Most bodybuilders will respond best to 2.3-3.1 g/kg of lean body mass of protein, 15-30% of calories from fat, and the remainder from carbohydrate.

whittaker-2021.title: Low-fat diets and testosterone in men: Systematic review and meta-analysis of intervention studies
whittaker-2021.journal: The Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
whittaker-2021.support: 6 eligible studies with 206 participants; significant decreases in sex hormones on low-fat vs high-fat diets (total testosterone SMD -0.38).

reynolds-2019.title: Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses
reynolds-2019.support: 185 prospective studies and 58 clinical trials with 4635 adult participants; risk reduction was greatest when daily intake of dietary fibre was between 25 g and 29 g.

savoie-2015.title: Effect of Hypohydration on Muscle Endurance, Strength, Anaerobic Power and Capacity and Vertical Jumping Ability: A Meta-Analysis
savoie-2015.support: 28 manuscripts; hypohydration impaired muscle endurance by 8.3%, strength fell by 5.5%, anaerobic power by 5.8%.

parr-2014.title: Alcohol Ingestion Impairs Maximal Post-Exercise Rates of Myofibrillar Protein Synthesis following a Single Bout of Concurrent Training
parr-2014.support: Compared to protein alone, there was a reduction in MPS with alcohol plus protein (24%) and alcohol plus carbohydrate (37%); 8 active males, 1.5 g/kg alcohol.

kwok-2019.title: Effect of alcohol consumption on food energy intake: a systematic review and meta-analysis
kwok-2019.support: 22 studies involving 701 participants; no compensation for alcoholic beverage energy; food energy intake rose 343 kJ and total energy 1072 kJ.

thomas-2016.title: Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and the American College of Sports Medicine: Nutrition and Athletic Performance
thomas-2016.journal: Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics
thomas-2016.support: Performance and recovery are enhanced by well-chosen nutrition strategies; guidelines for the appropriate type, amount, and timing of intake of food, fluids, and supplements.

kreider-2017.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation in exercise, sport, and medicine
kreider-2017.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
kreider-2017.support: Short and long-term supplementation (up to 30 g/day for 5 years) is safe and well-tolerated in healthy individuals.

delpino-2022.title: Influence of age, sex, and type of exercise on the efficacy of creatine supplementation on lean body mass: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
delpino-2022.support: 35 studies, 1192 participants; creatine with resistance training increased LBM by 1.10 kg; males +1.46 kg vs a non-significant 0.29 kg in females.

grgic-2018.title: Effects of caffeine intake on muscle strength and power: a systematic review and meta-analysis
grgic-2018.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
grgic-2018.support: Caffeine improved strength (SMD 0.20) and power (SMD 0.17); upper but not lower body strength.

trexler-2015.title: International society of sports nutrition position stand: Beta-Alanine
trexler-2015.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
trexler-2015.support: 4-6 g daily for at least 2-4 weeks improves exercise performance, with more pronounced effects in tasks lasting 1-4 min; paraesthesia is the only reported side effect.

varvik-2021.title: Acute Effect of Citrulline Malate on Repetition Performance During Strength Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
varvik-2021.journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
varvik-2021.support: Eight studies, 137 participants; 6-8 g citrulline malate 40-60 min before exercise increased repetitions by 3 (6.4%) vs placebo.

maughan-2018.title: IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete
maughan-2018.support: Only a few supplements (including caffeine, creatine, specific buffering agents and nitrate) have good evidence of benefits; inadvertent ingestion of prohibited substances is a known risk.

wolfe-2017.title: Branched-chain amino acids and muscle protein synthesis in humans: myth or reality?
wolfe-2017.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
wolfe-2017.support: No studies in human subjects quantified the MPS response to orally ingested BCAAs alone; two intravenous studies found BCAAs decreased muscle protein synthesis.

clemesha-2020.title: ‘Testosterone Boosting’ Supplements Composition and Claims Are not Supported by the Academic Literature
clemesha-2020.journal: The World Journal of Men's Health
clemesha-2020.support: Fifty T-booster supplements; no data on testosterone for 61.5% of supplements; 24.8% had data showing an increase.

frankenfield-2005.title: Comparison of Predictive Equations for Resting Metabolic Rate in Healthy Nonobese and Obese Adults: A Systematic Review
frankenfield-2005.journal: Journal of the American Dietetic Association
frankenfield-2005.support: Mifflin-St Jeor was the most reliable, predicting RMR within 10% of measured in more nonobese and obese individuals than the other equations.

hall-2011.title: Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight
hall-2011.support: Bodyweight response to a change of energy intake is slow, with half times of about 1 year; a small persistent gap of about 30 kJ per day underlies observed average weight gain.

hall-2019.title: Ultra-Processed Diets Cause Excess Calorie Intake and Weight Gain: An Inpatient Randomized Controlled Trial of Ad Libitum Food Intake
hall-2019.support: 20 weight-stable adults; weight changes were highly correlated with energy intake (r = 0.8); +0.9 kg on ultra-processed vs -0.9 kg on unprocessed diet.

fao-2004.title: Human energy requirements: report of a joint FAO/WHO/UNU expert consultation
fao-2004.support: The PAL values that can be sustained for a long period of time by free-living adult populations range from about 1.40 to 2.40.

fao-2003.title: Food energy: methods of analysis and conversion factors (Chapter 3: Calculation of the energy content of foods)
fao-2003.support: Energy values are 17 kJ/g (4.0 kcal/g) for protein, 37 kJ/g (9.0 kcal/g) for fat and 17 kJ/g (4.0 kcal/g) for carbohydrates; alcohol 29 kJ/g (7.0 kcal/g).

cfr-101-9.title: 21 CFR 101.9 Nutrition labeling of food, paragraph (g)(5)
cfr-101-9.support: A food with a label declaration of calories ... shall be deemed misbranded if the nutrient content of the composite is greater than 20 percent in excess of the value declared on the label.

jumpertz-2013.title: Food label accuracy of common snack foods
jumpertz-2013.support: 24 popular snack products; metabolizable calories 4.3% higher than the label statement (median), overall well within FDA limits.

urban-2011.title: Accuracy of Stated Energy Contents of Restaurant Foods
urban-2011.support: 269 items from 42 restaurants; 50 (19%) contained at least 100 kcal/portion more than stated.

urban-2010.title: The Accuracy of Stated Energy Contents of Reduced-Energy, Commercially Prepared Foods
urban-2010.journal: Journal of the American Dietetic Association
urban-2010.support: 29 restaurant foods averaged 18% more energy than stated and 10 frozen meals 8% more; free side dishes raised energy to an average of 245% of stated values for the entrees.

urban-2016.title: Energy Contents of Frequently Ordered Restaurant Meals and Comparison with Human Energy Requirements and US Department of Agriculture Database Information: A Multisite Randomized Study
urban-2016.journal: Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics
urban-2016.support: Meals from non-chain restaurants contained 1,205 +/- 465 kcal/meal, not significantly different from equivalent large-chain meals.

evenepoel-2020.title: Accuracy of Nutrient Calculations Using the Consumer-Focused Online App MyFitnessPal: Validation Study
evenepoel-2020.support: 50 participants kept 4-day records twice; cleaned MyFitnessPal values correlated strongly with the Belgian database for energy (r=0.96); cleaning removed 2.8% of entries; upper limit of 1500 kcal per portion.

griffiths-2018.title: Assessment of the accuracy of nutrient calculations of five popular nutrition tracking applications
griffiths-2018.support: Thirty 24-h recalls entered into five apps; correlations 0.73 to 0.96 for energy and macronutrients; for each app one or more mean nutrient values were significantly lower than the research software.

burrows-2019.title: Validity of Dietary Assessment Methods When Compared to the Method of Doubly Labeled Water: A Systematic Review in Adults
burrows-2019.support: 59 studies with 6,298 free living adults; the majority reported significant under-reporting of energy intake compared with doubly labeled water.

capling-2017.title: Validity of Dietary Assessment in Athletes: A Systematic Review
capling-2017.support: Self-reported energy intake in athletes was under-estimated by 19% against doubly labelled water (11 studies).

lichtman-1992.title: Discrepancy between Self-Reported and Actual Caloric Intake and Exercise in Obese Subjects
lichtman-1992.support: Subjects with a history of diet resistance under-reported actual food intake by 47 +/- 16 percent and over-reported physical activity by 51 percent.

champagne-2002.title: Energy Intake and Energy Expenditure
champagne-2002.journal: Journal of the American Dietetic Association
champagne-2002.support: 10 dietitians and 10 controls; the dietitians under-reported energy intake by 223 kcal/day and controls by 429 kcal/day against doubly labeled water.

authors: Washington University School of Medicine CALERIE Team
racette-2008.title: Influence of Weekend Lifestyle Patterns on Body Weight
racette-2008.support: 48 adults; participants gained weight on weekend days at baseline; on weekends calorie-restricted participants stopped losing weight.

orsama-2014.title: Weight Rhythms: Weight Increases during Weekends and Decreases during Weekdays
orsama-2014.support: Daily weights of 80 adults, 4,657 measurements; higher weight on Sunday and Monday, decreasing during the week.

harvey-2019.title: Log Often, Lose More: Electronic Dietary Self‐Monitoring for Weight Loss
harvey-2019.support: 142 participants in a 24-week online program; those losing >=5% of weight logged in more times per day (2.4 vs 1.6).

burke-2011sm.title: Self-Monitoring in Weight Loss: A Systematic Review of the Literature
burke-2011sm.journal: Journal of the American Dietetic Association
burke-2011sm.support: 22 studies; a significant association between self-monitoring and weight loss was consistently found; the level of evidence was weak because of methodologic limitations.

levinson-2017.title: My Fitness Pal calorie tracker usage in the eating disorders
levinson-2017.support: 105 individuals diagnosed with an eating disorder; ~75% used My Fitness Pal and 73% of these perceived the app as contributing to their eating disorder.

linardon-2019.title: My fitness pal usage in men: Associations with eating disorder symptoms and psychosocial impairment
linardon-2019.support: 122 men; MFP users reported significantly higher levels of eating disorder symptoms than non-users.
